acquisition.why: No channel is specified. The make-money-online audience is reached mainly through paid social and content, which is crowded and expensive [E]. A solo part-timer has no existing audience to draw on.

onboarding.why: Self-serve sign-up and an AI-generated plan work unattended.

delivery.why: LLM plans and push notifications are software. Prompt tuning and quality drift still need occasional checks.

billing.why: Stripe or app-store subscriptions run unattended. The 'card-on-file penalties' feature invites disputes, chargebacks and consumer-law risk.

support.why: Users who see it as a magic pill and then blame it will generate refund and complaint traffic. Agents can handle most of this.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build it technically. However, consumer subscription churn in make-money-online is brutal, and penalty charges raise UK consumer-protection (CMA/DMCC) issues. Generic ChatGPT/Claude can already act as an 'AI co-founder' for free [E].
scores.M_why: Heavily commoditised by general LLM assistants and a flood of AI-coach apps in 2026. There is no moat.
scores.one_line: The source is one hypothetical riff with no first-hand evidence. It is an easily built but thin LLM wrapper in a high-churn, saturated make-money-online niche, so it is unattractive.

acquisition.why: Etsy search and Etsy Ads are inbound and UK-legal. The idea depends heavily on Etsy's algorithm and terms.

onboarding.why: Buyers onboard themselves; there is no onboarding.

delivery.why: Etsy delivers instant downloads automatically. Agents can generate designs and mock-ups, but quality, text rendering and IP checks need human review.

billing.why: Etsy handles payments, and VAT on digital sales in many cases.

support.why: Messages are mostly file-access questions that agents can template. The occasional review dispute needs a human.

scores.R_why: It fits a £300 budget and 6-8 h/week. A UK seller can run it on Etsy. Avoid copying best-sellers, because that risks IP takedowns, and avoid buying accounts, which breaches Etsy's terms.
scores.M_why: The market is flooded with AI-generated printables in 2026. Etsy is cracking down on low-effort AI listings and per-product earnings are small (~$20/month claimed). Platform risk is high.
scores.one_line: It is highly automatable and cheap to test via Etsy inbound, but extreme AI saturation and platform dependence make returns small and fragile.

acquisition.why: A quiz is a lead magnet and needs traffic from somewhere. The sources rely on an existing podcast audience; without one, Ricardo would need SEO or ads.

onboarding.why: Self-serve quiz with an email gate.

delivery.why: LLM-generated results run unattended. Recommendation content needs periodic updates as AI models change.

billing.why: There is no monetisation in the source, so there is nothing to bill until a downstream offer exists.

support.why: Free tool; support needs are minimal.

scores.R_why: It is easy to build in a few hours. However, it is a funnel component, not a business, and there is no revenue model. UK GDPR and PECR require explicit consent for follow-up marketing emails.
scores.M_why: Quiz lead magnets are common, and AI-model-picker content is commoditised and goes stale fast [E].
scores.one_line: This is a useful tactic for capturing emails, but it is not a standalone agent-run business because it has neither monetisation nor its own traffic source.

acquisition.why: It works only through the host's established YouTube channel. Ricardo has no audience, and building one takes far more than 6-8 h/week to get traction [E].

delivery.why: Recorded course content is static. It must be re-recorded frequently as Base44 changes.

billing.why: Stripe or a course platform handles billing.

support.why: Student how-to questions can mostly be answered by agents using course material.

scores.R_why: The $499 price is an anchor: the course is given away free as a lead magnet, so it is not real revenue evidence. Ricardo lacks the audience or creator brand, and the course is tied to a single vendor that changes quickly.
scores.M_why: Courses on no-code and vibe-coding are saturated in 2026. Vendors' own free tutorials and AI assistants substitute for them, and the dependence on Base44 is high.
scores.one_line: The claims are promotional anchors from a creator selling to his own audience. Without an audience this course business doesn't transfer to Ricardo.

acquisition.why: Gumroad, Etsy and SEO are inbound channels. The cited $3k came mainly from an existing audience and newsletter, which Ricardo lacks. Marketplaces help but add platform dependence.

onboarding.why: Purchase followed by a download page.

delivery.why: Agents can write and test skills or prompts. A human needs to check quality and update the packs as models change.

billing.why: Stripe or Gumroad, one-off payments. UK digital-goods VAT and a cancellation-rights waiver are needed.

support.why: 'It doesn't work in my setup' questions are mostly agent-answerable, but some refunds will need judgement.

scores.R_why: It matches Ricardo's technical skills and costs almost nothing to test within £300. Without an audience, sales will be far below the claimed $3k/month [E]. Avoid finance or investing skills because of FCA financial-promotion concerns.
scores.M_why: Packs are easily copied and Anthropic and OpenAI ship free skills. Product life is short, though niche domain-expert skills have some headroom [E].
scores.one_line: It is a cheap, fully digital test that suits Ricardo. Commoditisation and audience dependence cap the upside, so niche domain skills sold through marketplaces and SEO are the best angle.

acquisition.why: App Store search plus paid Meta ads are legal inbound channels. The cited successes relied on daily founder content or 500-account UGC farms, which are labour-intensive and risk platform bans.

onboarding.why: App-store install and an in-app paywall.

delivery.why: Software, but it needs continuous iteration and app-review cycles. Bugs need developer attention.

billing.why: App Store and RevenueCat handle billing.

support.why: Agents can answer app-store reviews and support email. Health-data and safety queries need care.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build it with Claude Code and Expo. Winning in this market requires heavy content or ad spend that £300 and 6-8 h/week can't fund. UK GDPR treats health data as special-category data, and nutrition, supplement or peptide features add risk.
scores.M_why: Extremely saturated (Strong, Hevy, Fitbod and hundreds of AI clones). The one example's edge was language localisation, not product.
scores.one_line: The revenue is first-hand and plausible, but it comes from intense founder content and UGC in a saturated market. A well-automated product does not overcome acquisition costs that are out of reach for Ricardo.

acquisition.why: Bolt's growth came from a seven-year team, a pre-built community and virality. A niche wrapper would need content or ads to get users.

delivery.why: A white-label wrapper runs on Lovable or Replit, but generated apps break. The proposed upsell to human engineers is manual.

billing.why: Stripe subscriptions work, but they are exposed to the cost of LLM inference passed through from the underlying platform.

support.why: Users debugging generated apps produce heavy, technical support load.

scores.R_why: Bolt's $20M ARR is irrelevant to a solo builder. A niche wrapper (for example kids' game building) adds child-safety and Children's Code obligations in the UK. Its margins depend on upstream pricing.
scores.M_why: Lovable, Bolt, Replit and others dominate, and the underlying platforms add niche templates themselves. Wrapper risk is extreme.
scores.one_line: The headline is an outlier venture-scale success that doesn't transfer. The solo version is a thin wrapper with heavy support load and no moat.

acquisition.why: The WordPress.org directory and SEO are inbound. Ranking tactics are dated and the channel depends on the platform.

onboarding.why: Install from the directory, then licence activation.

delivery.why: Code maintenance, compatibility updates and security patches can be agent-assisted. A human developer must review releases.

billing.why: Freemius, Lemon Squeezy or Stripe licensing runs unattended.

support.why: Agents can handle the bulk of support-forum and ticket traffic. Edge-case conflicts need a human.

scores.R_why: It suits Ricardo's technical skills and agent-assisted maintenance. However, £300 cannot buy a plugin with meaningful MRR, which typically sells for 2-4x annual profit [E], and due diligence takes time. Ricardo could only buy a tiny or abandoned plugin.
scores.M_why: There is a long tail of neglected plugins and micro-SaaS on the Acquire and Flippa marketplaces. WordPress market share is slowly eroding and AI builders compete, but niche utility plugins persist.
scores.one_line: This is one of the more agent-friendly models: inbound distribution, software delivery and recurring licences. It is capital-constrained at £300 and supported by a single first-hand source.
